Words that begin with the /wr/ consonant blend sound the same as words that begin with /r/.
In English, you will often encounter silent letters. One example is words that begin with /wr/ where the w is silent.
Look at the table below that shows one word starting with /wr/ and a similar word starting with /r/. The pronunciation is the same.

carefully formed or shaped iron designs
Example: Where can I buy a wrought iron lamp?
These are words you use to talk about managing a restaurant.
someone who is a mess; showing strain from being overtired and overworked
Example: Vanessa looked like a wreck from the stress at work.
to twist and rub your hands together because you are nervous or upset
Example: Vanessa was wringing her hands because she was nervous about the video call with the owner.
a small line or fold that appears on your skin as you grow older (usually used in the plural)
Example: She thinks the stress from her job is putting wrinkles on her face.
to make your brain suffer from thinking too hard
Example: Vanessa didn't want to wrack/rack her brain by herself writing the safety policy.
an article, usually a review, that appears in an informal magazine
Example: There was a write-up about Bistro 88 in the local magazine.
Find a write-up in a magazine or website for a local restaurant that you have been to.
Read the write-up article. Then rewrite it with your own opinion of the restaurant.
Use as many phrasal verbs as you can.
Share your review with your partner.
I read and understand a review of a local restaurant.
I write my own review of a local establishment.

images.text:
Vanessa: Hello, Bistro 88, Vanessa speaking.
Caller: Hi. How much is a wrought iron lamp?
Vanessa: I think you've got the wrong number.
Caller: Oh, my friend passed on this number to me. Is this 617-555-1740?
Vanessa: No, it's 1440.
Caller: Oh, sorry about that.

Vanessa: No problem. Oh, goodness.
Assistant Manager: Vanessa, you look like a wreck. Are you okay?
Vanessa: Oh, I'm so tired from all the phone calls. That was another wrong number. Sometimes I just want to hang up on them. I still have to call up the restaurant owner on video.
Assistant Manager: You're wringing your hands. Are you worried about the call? Maybe you should take a break.

Vanessa: No, I still have to rewrite the safety policy because I forgot to save it. I swear I'm starting to put wrinkles on my face.
Assistant Manager: Oh, no. Well, I've written something similar before. Can I help?
Vanessa: Oh, that would be much appreciated. That way, I don't have to wrack my brain on the wording. Thanks.
Assistant Manager: Hey, did you see the write-up of our restaurant in Cambridge Life magazine?
Vanessa: Oh, I think my friend Sally wrote it. I must read it.
